title: Above the trees at Kakum: Ghana's canopy walk and how to do it right
excerpt: Forty metres up, on seven swaying bridges strung between the tallest trees in the forest, you walk right through the top of Ghana's rainforest. Kakum National Park sits a short drive north of Cape Coast, and the koach thinks it is the perfect morning to pair with the castles. Here is how to time it, what actually lives down in that green, and how to walk the canopy without the crowds.
heroAlt: A single rope-and-plank suspension bridge of the Kakum canopy walkway strung high between tall forest trees, morning mist rising off an unbroken green rainforest canopy below in Ghana's Central Region
author: TripKoach

body.x: Akwaaba. Most people come to Ghana's Central Region for the castles, and they should. But an hour up the road from the coast, the land climbs into thick, green, dripping rainforest, and above that forest hangs one of the most famous walks in all of Africa. This week the koach takes you off the sand and forty metres up into the treetops at Kakum. Bring your nerve and your quietest voice, and let the koach show you the canopy.
What Kakum actually is

Kakum National Park protects about 375 square kilometres of Upper Guinean rainforest, one of the last big stretches of this forest type left in West Africa. It sits in the Central Region, roughly a 45 minute drive north of Cape Coast on the road toward Kruwa and the interior. The area was first set aside as a reserve back in 1931 and became a full national park in 1992, once surveys showed just how much still lived under that canopy.

And plenty lives under it. Kakum holds the densest population of forest elephants in Ghana, along with bongo antelope, several kinds of duiker, and monkeys including the shy Diana monkey. Birders come for the count: more than 260 recorded species, nine kinds of hornbill, and the grey parrot among them. Add over 500 species of butterfly and you get a forest that is loud with life even when you cannot see a single large animal.

The koach will be honest with you here, because that matters. The big animals are elusive. Forest elephants move at night and keep deep in the trees, and most day visitors never see one. Do not come to Kakum for a safari. Come for the forest itself, for the birdsong at dawn, for the butterflies on the path, and above all for the walk in the sky.
The canopy walkway

This is the reason Kakum is on every Ghana list. The canopy walkway is a chain of seven rope-and-plank suspension bridges, strung end to end between the crowns of the tallest trees, running about 350 metres in total and hanging some 40 metres above the forest floor. It was built in 1995 and remains one of very few walks of its kind anywhere in Africa.

It is safe. The bridges are aluminium ladder and wooden plank underfoot, wire rope and netting at the sides, and the park keeps them checked. But safe does not mean still. The bridges sway and dip as you move, the ground drops away beneath the netting, and there is a moment on the first span where your legs will have an opinion about all this. That is the whole point. Push through it and by the third bridge you are grinning, looking out over an unbroken green roof of forest with birds crossing below you.

You reach the walkway on a short but steep guided climb up through the forest, maybe 20 to 30 minutes, on a proper trail. Park guides lead every group and point out trees, medicinal plants and whatever is calling in the branches. The koach says listen to them. They know this forest.
When to go, and the green season truth

Kakum is rainforest, so it rains. That is what makes it green and alive, and it is also what you plan around. The koach's rule is simple: go early. The park opens around dawn, and the first slot of the morning is the one you want. The light is soft, the air is cool, the birds are busy, and the walkway is quiet before the tour buses arrive from Cape Coast and Accra.

Come for the opening and you get the canopy almost to yourself. Come at 11am on a Saturday and you get a queue on the first bridge. Early also means you beat the heat of the climb and the heaviest rain, which tends to build later in the day. If a downpour comes through, the walkway closes for safety until it passes, so a dawn start gives you the best odds of walking dry.

For our friends coming during the green season, Kakum is arguably at its best. The forest is at full volume, the mist sits in the valleys at first light, and the crowds are thinner. Just bring a light rain layer and shoes that grip.
Make it a proper Central Region day

Here is how the koach would build the day. Kakum pairs naturally with the coast, because it sits so close to it. Do the canopy walk at opening, when you are fresh and the forest is quiet, then drive back down to the coast for the afternoon and stand inside the castles at Cape Coast and Elmina. Treetops in the morning, history by the sea after lunch. It is one of the finest single days in the whole country.

If you are basing yourself in the capital, this works as a long day trip, but the koach would rather you slept a night on the coast so you are not rushing. Get your bearings in the city first with our guide to your first 24 hours in Accra, then head west to the Central Region with time to do it slowly.

Practical notes from the koach: - Wear closed shoes with grip. The climb to the walkway is steep and can be slick after rain. Leave the sandals in the car. - Bring water and a small bag. It is humid work, and there is nowhere to buy much up on the trail. - Fees are paid at the gate and there are separate rates for the park and the canopy walkway, with lower prices for residents. They get reviewed from time to time, so check the current rate when you arrive rather than trusting an old figure online. - Keep your voice down on the bridges. It is a wildlife park, not a fairground, and quiet groups see and hear far more. - Guides are included and worth it. Ask questions. That is how a good walk becomes a great one.

Stand in the middle of that fourth bridge, high over the forest, with nothing but green in every direction and a hornbill flapping past below you, and you understand why people cross the world for this. The koach just wants you to do it early, do it slow, and do it right.
Ready to walk the treetops? Tell the koach when you are coming and we will build the whole Central Region day around it.

title: Surf, forts and a village on the water: a long weekend on Ghana's western coast
excerpt: West of the castles, past the last big town, Ghana's coast slows right down. This week the koach takes you to Busua for the country's best surf, out to the old forts and the southernmost tip at Cape Three Points, and finally by dugout canoe to Nzulezu, a whole village built on stilts over a quiet lake.
heroAlt: Small wooden fishing canoes drawn up on the golden sand of Busua beach in Ghana's Western Region at low tide, green palm-covered headland behind and a soft rainy-season swell rolling in
author: TripKoach

body.x: Akwaaba. Last week the koach had you an hour from Accra, watching baboons cross the road at Shai Hills. This week the koach is taking you all the way to the other end of the map, out past Cape Coast, past the last big city, to the long green coast in Ghana's far west. This is where the country exhales. Surf towns, sleepy fishing villages, old forts falling into the palms, and a whole community that lives on stilts over a lake. Pack light, leave your rush in Accra, and let the koach show you the western coast.
The coast most visitors never reach

Everybody comes to Ghana's central coast for the castles at Cape Coast and Elmina, and rightly so, because that story has to be felt in person. But most travellers stop there and turn back east. Keep going west and the coast keeps getting quieter, greener and slower, all the way to the border with Cote d'Ivoire.

The hub of it all is Sekondi-Takoradi, the twin harbour city usually just called Takoradi, or "Tadi" to everyone who lives there. It is Ghana's western anchor, a few hours by road from Cape Coast or a short domestic hop from Accra, and it is where the koach points you first. From Tadi the good stuff is all within reach: the surf at Busua, the forts on their headlands, the lighthouse at the end of the country, and the canoe ride to Nzulezu. This is a coast that rewards a proper long weekend, not a rushed day.
Busua: Ghana's surf town

An hour or so west of Takoradi, the road drops down to Busua, and something in you unclenches. Busua is a small crescent of golden sand between two green headlands, a fishing village at one end and a string of easy beach places along the shore. It is, without much argument, the surf capital of Ghana.

The waves here are friendly. Busua breaks gently enough for a complete beginner to stand up on their first morning, but with enough shape further out to keep improving surfers happy. There are locally run surf schools right on the sand where you can rent a board and take a lesson from Ghanaian surfers who grew up in these waters, and the koach will always steer you to those local outfits first. Even if you never touch a board, Busua is the kind of place where the day organises itself: a swim, grilled fish and rice, a walk to the fishing end to watch the canoes come in, a cold drink as the sun goes down over the water. Time behaves differently here.

At low tide you can wade and walk across to tiny Busua island just offshore, a five minute paddle with a ruined little chapel on top and a big view back over the bay. Ask a local about the tide before you go and do not get caught out on the way back.
Butre, Dixcove and the old forts
The western coast is stitched with forts, the same trading forts that run all the way along Ghana's shore, and out here they sit quiet and half-wild instead of polished for crowds.

A short walk or ride from Busua brings you to Dixcove, a busy working fishing harbour crowned by Fort Metal Cross, a white British fort from the late 1600s looking down on the boats. Just the other side of Busua lies Butre, one of the prettiest spots on the whole coast, where a lagoon and river meet the sea under the ruins of the Dutch Fort Batenstein on the hill. You can take a small canoe up the Butre lagoon through the mangroves, climb up to the crumbling fort for the view, and understand in a few quiet minutes why people fall for this stretch of coast. There is no ticket booth theatre here. It is just the sea, the river, the old stones and the birds.
Cape Three Points: the end of Ghana

Push a little further and you reach Cape Three Points, the southernmost tip of the whole country. This is the headland closest to the point where the equator and the prime meridian cross out at sea, so locals will tell you, with a grin, that you are standing at "the nearest land to the centre of the world."

On the point sits a small lighthouse, built in 1925 and still keeping watch, with a caretaker who will usually let you climb up for a 360 degree sweep of rainforest on one side and open Atlantic on the other. Around it is a patch of coastal forest full of birds and monkeys. It feels like the end of the road because it more or less is. The koach loves bringing people here for that exact feeling: the sense of having reached the far edge of Ghana and found it green, wild and almost empty.
Nzulezu: the village on the water
Now for the one that stays with people. Further west again, near the town of Beyin in the Jomoro District, the koach puts you in a dugout canoe and paddles you off the land entirely.

About an hour up a channel through reeds and water lilies, the waterway opens onto quiet Lake Tadane, and there, standing on stilts and wooden platforms right over the water, is a whole village. This is Nzulezu, which means "surface of water" in the Nzema language. Around five hundred people live here, in stilted houses linked by a central raised walkway, with a school, a chapel and a shrine, all built above the lake. The people trace their arrival to a long migration out of the old empires of the interior, and their traditions, tied closely to the lake and its rules, have been kept alive here for generations.

Nzulezu has sat on Ghana's UNESCO World Heritage tentative list since 2000, recognised as a rare surviving stilt settlement and a masterpiece of adapting human life to water. Visiting is done with respect: you come with a guide from the visitor centre at Beyin, you keep to the walkways, you ask before you photograph people and homes, and you remember this is a living community and not a display. Glide in on that canoe, step up onto the wooden platform, and you will not forget it.
How the koach would shape the weekend
Give the western coast a long weekend, three nights if you can. A shape the koach likes:

x: Get to Takoradi first, by the coastal road through Cape Coast, or a quick domestic flight from Accra to save the day.
Settle in at Busua for two nights. Surf or swim, walk to Dixcove and Fort Metal Cross, and give an afternoon to Butre's lagoon and hilltop fort.
Run out to Cape Three Points for a morning to climb the lighthouse and stand at the bottom of the country.
Make the trip to Nzulezu near Beyin, further west, for the canoe ride and the stilt village. It is a longer drive, so give it its own unhurried day.

body.x: You can do all of this by public transport and shared taxi if you like an adventure, or tell the koach your dates and the koach will line up the ride, the timing and the tides so nothing is rushed and nothing is missed.
The honest green-season note

Here is the twist the koach loves. You are reading this deep in Ghana's green season, and on most of this blog the koach gently argues that the low season is a feature, not a bug. On the western coast it is more than that. Ghana's surf season runs roughly from April into late September, which means the green months are not the off season out here at all. They are prime time. The swell is working, the hills are their greenest, and the beaches are yours.

Be honest with yourself about the rain, though, because the far west is one of the wettest corners of the country. You will catch showers. They tend to sweep in, drum on the roof, and move off to leave everything washed and glowing. Bring a light rain layer, dry bags for your phone and camera, reef-safe sunscreen, and shoes you do not mind getting wet on the forts and the canoe. Respect the sea, swim where locals swim, and ask about currents before you go out.
Slot it into your Ghana trip

The beauty of the western coast is that it is the natural next chapter after the places the koach has already shown you. Land in Accra and find your feet in the first day or two. Feel the weight of history at Cape Coast and Elmina. Then, instead of turning back, keep going west into the surf, the forts and the stilt village, where Ghana slows all the way down.

If the estuary weekend at Ada is where Ghana's rivers meet the sea in the east, the western coast is where the country quietly runs out of road in the west, and saves its best beaches for the people who bother to go looking.
Do not turn back at Cape Coast. Tell the koach how long you have, and the koach will carry you all the way west.

title: Baboons before lunch: a wildlife day trip to Shai Hills, an hour from Accra
excerpt: You do not need to fly north to Mole to see wild animals in Ghana. An hour up the road from Accra, baboons cross in front of your car, zebras graze under granite hills, and sacred caves hold the memory of a whole people. Here is the koach's guide to a half-day safari at Shai Hills, the capital's easiest escape into the wild.
heroAlt: A dirt track winding across the dry savanna plain of Shai Hills Resource Reserve toward the reserve's tree-covered granite inselbergs, scattered trees dotting the golden-green grassland under a pale, lightly clouded sky
author: TripKoach

body.x: Akwaaba. Last time the koach kept you in the capital for the drums of Homowo. This week the koach is getting you back out of the city, but only just. An hour up the road, no flight, no long haul north, there is a place where baboons cross the track in front of your car and grey granite hills rise straight out of the grass. It is called Shai Hills, and it is the easiest wild day out you will find anywhere near Accra. Let the koach take you.
The capital's back-garden safari

Most people think you have to make the long journey up to Mole in the far north to see animals in Ghana, and the koach has written you that trip because it is worth every one of those hours. But you do not have to. The Shai Hills Resource Reserve sits in the Greater Accra Region, roughly an hour northeast of the city on the Accra to Akosombo road, just past Dodowa near Doryumu. It is the closest protected wildlife area to the capital, and you can be walking among baboons before you would normally have finished your second coffee.

The reserve is a stretch of coastal savanna, open golden grassland studded with a handful of dramatic granite hills that push up out of the flat plain like the backs of sleeping animals. It is looked after by the Wildlife Division of Ghana's Forestry Commission. It is not a manicured zoo and it is not a luxury game park. It is a real, working reserve, and that is exactly why the koach loves sending people here for a first taste of wild Ghana close to home.
What you will actually see

The stars of Shai Hills are the baboons. A large troop of olive baboons lives near the entrance and along the internal roads, and they are relaxed, bold and completely used to vehicles. It is very common to round a bend and find a family of them sitting in the road, grooming, arguing, carrying babies on their backs. It is a genuine thrill the first time, and the koach never gets tired of it.

Beyond the baboons, keep your eyes open for green (vervet) monkeys in the trees, kob and bushbuck antelope stepping through the grass, and, on the open plains, the reserve's introduced zebras and ostriches. Sightings of those two are never guaranteed, the way nothing wild ever is, but a patient morning with a good guide gives you a real chance. Shai Hills is also a lovely spot for birds, with a long species list across the grassland, the hills and the wooded patches, so bring binoculars if you carry them.

What you will not find here are elephants or big cats. This is a gentle, safe reserve, which makes it perfect for families, for first-timers, and for anyone who wants the shape of a safari without the distance or the drama.
More than animals: the sacred caves
Here is the part that lifts Shai Hills above a simple animal-spotting trip. Those granite hills are hollow with history.

The reserve is named for the Shai people, who once lived up on these hills, farming the plains below and taking shelter in the caves and rock overhangs among the boulders. The caves held shrines, homes and gathering places, a whole community woven into the stone. Then in 1892 the colonial administration forced the Shai off their hills and down onto the plains, and the reserve you drive through today is, in part, the emptied home they left behind. The Shai still return for traditional rites.

A guided walk up to the caves and rock shelters is the soul of a Shai Hills visit. You scramble up between huge granite boulders, duck into cool cave mouths where bats wheel in the dark, and stand on high ground looking out over the whole shimmering plain toward Accra. Your guide will tell you which caves were sacred, how the community lived up here, and why the hills still matter to the Shai. It is the same lesson the koach keeps coming back to on this blog: in Ghana the land and the people's story are never far apart.
How the koach would spend the morning

Shai Hills is an easy half-day, and the koach's strong advice is to go early. Leave Accra soon after dawn, both to beat the heat and because the animals are most active in the cool of the morning. A rough shape for the day:

x: Roll in early and stop at the gate, where you pay your reserve fees and pick up a mandatory guide. You cannot wander the reserve or the caves alone, and honestly you would not want to.
Do a slow game drive along the internal tracks with your guide reading the grass, looking for antelope, monkeys and the plains animals, and of course meeting the baboons.
Hike up to the caves for the history, the bats and the view. Wear proper shoes, this is a real little scramble over rock.
Be back in the city for lunch, which is the beauty of the whole thing. You can have a wild morning and still make an afternoon meeting in Osu.

body.x: Fitter, more adventurous koach travellers can add rock climbing or a longer hike among the inselbergs, and cyclists can arrange to ride the tracks. Tell the koach what you are after and the koach will shape the morning to fit.
The honest green-season note

You are reading this in the middle of Ghana's green season, and the koach will always be straight with you about what that means. Shai Hills sits in the drier coastal savanna belt, so it does not get the heavy forest rains of the south, but you may still catch a warm shower this time of year. That is good news, not bad. The grass is green, the hills are at their most beautiful, the light is soft, and the crowds are thin. A passing rain just clears the heat and moves on. As the koach keeps saying, travelling in the low season is a feature, not a bug.

Bring water, a hat, sunscreen, sturdy shoes for the caves, and insect repellent. Keep your car windows up around the baboons and never, ever feed them, a fed baboon is a bold baboon, and that helps nobody. Beyond that, come with an easy morning and an open mind.
Slot it into your Accra week

The real gift of Shai Hills is how neatly it drops into a capital trip. You do not have to build a whole expedition around it. Land in Accra, spend your first day or two finding your feet in the city, give one cool afternoon to the botanical gardens up at Aburi, and then give one early morning to the baboons and caves of Shai Hills. Three completely different faces of Greater Accra, all within an hour of your hotel: the living city, the green hills, and the wild plain.

That is the koach's whole philosophy in one week. Ghana rewards the traveller who slows down and looks close to home before racing off to the far corners. The far corners are wonderful, and the koach will take you to every one of them. But there are wild baboons and sacred caves an hour from the airport, and most visitors drive straight past them.
Do not be most visitors. Tell the koach your dates, and the koach will line up the guide, the timing and the ride, and have you back in the city before the day gets hot.

title: Hooting at hunger: how to catch Homowo, Accra's own harvest festival
excerpt: Every August the Ga people of Accra throw a festival that literally jeers at famine. It has a sacred quiet before it and an explosion of drumming, kpokpoi and twins in white after it. Here is the koach's guide to experiencing Homowo in the capital with respect, and to timing your first Ghana trip around it.
heroAlt: A Homowo procession in Teshie, Accra: Ga traditional priests and celebrants in white cloth draped with green herb garlands, bare-shouldered priests bent low over their ritual staffs with white markings on their faces, a dense crowd behind them in warm afternoon light
author: TripKoach

body.x: Akwaaba. For the last few weeks the koach has been driving you out of the city, to estuaries and elephants and castles down the coast. This week we do something different. This week we stay in Accra, and we listen to the capital throw a party at hunger's expense.

The festival is called Homowo, and the name is the whole story. In Ga, the language of Accra's founding people, it means roughly hooting at hunger. It is the harvest festival of the Ga people of Greater Accra, and it is one of the great living celebrations of this country, held not in a museum but in the streets of Jamestown, La, Teshie, Nungua, Osu and Tema every year. If you want to feel the real, ceremonial, family heart of Accra, Homowo is when the city shows it to you. Let the koach walk you in.
Where the name comes from

Long ago, when the Ga migrated down to these coastal plains, the story goes that they hit a terrible famine. People went hungry. Then the rains came right, the crops came in, and the harvest was so good that the people threw a feast and openly jeered at the hunger that had haunted them. That defiant laugh at famine is Homowo: a harvest thanksgiving, yes, but with an edge of triumph. Every year since, the Ga have marked the good harvest by hooting at the memory of the bad times.
The koach loves this festival for exactly that reason. It is not a solemn commemoration. It is gratitude with a swagger.
The quiet before the noise

Here is the part most visitors do not know, and it tells you how seriously the Ga take this season. Before Homowo comes a ban on drumming and noise-making across the Ga traditional area. For a stretch of weeks earlier in the year, the Ga Traditional Council asks the whole community to keep the peace: no drumming, no loud music, loudspeakers turned down, so that the land can rest and the people can pray for good rains and a full harvest. It is a period of quiet and reflection, and it is observed right across the capital.

That silence is the coiled spring. When the ban lifts and the harvest is blessed, the sound that was held back for weeks comes roaring out all at once, and the drums do not stop for days. If you have read the koach's guide to your first 24 hours in Accra, picture that same city, but with every neighbourhood drumming at once. That is Homowo.
What actually happens

Homowo is not one single day. It rolls out across the Ga towns over several weeks, each town keeping its own date, so the celebration ripples along the coast rather than landing all at once. But wherever you catch it, you will meet the same handful of beautiful traditions.

The kpokpoi and the sprinkling. The dish of the festival is kpokpoi (some call it kpekple), a steamed, gently fermented corn meal, eaten with a rich palm-nut soup and fish. On the main day the traditional priests, the Wulomei, walk through the town sprinkling kpokpoi on the ground to bless the land, feed the ancestors and share the harvest with the spirits of the place. Watching an elder scatter the sacred food along a Jamestown lane, murmuring blessings, is the quiet centre of the whole loud festival.

The twins. The Ga hold twins in special honour, and Homowo season includes a celebration for them, often called the Twins Yam Festival. Twins and multiple-birth children dress in white, are feasted and paraded, and are showered with attention and blessing. A street full of children in white, drumming and dancing, is one of the festival's most joyful sights.

The homecoming. Like the best festivals anywhere, Homowo is when Ga families come home. Relatives who live abroad or upcountry travel back to the family house, elders reconcile quarrels, and the extended family eats together. There is a warm, open-door, everyone-at-the-table feeling to the whole season that the koach finds genuinely moving.

The kpanlogo and the procession. Then there is the sheer noise and colour: kpanlogo drumming, dancing in the streets, chiefs carried in state in rich kente, and processions winding through the old coastal quarters. This is Accra with its whole heart out in the open.
When to come, and the honest date situation

Homowo falls in August, spread across the month as each Ga town takes its turn, so there is usually a Saturday somewhere in the Ga area celebrating through the second half of the month and into early September. Central Accra, Ga Mashie, is the one most visitors aim for.

The koach will be straight with you, the way the koach always is: the exact dates shift a little year to year and are set by the traditional authorities, not by a fixed calendar. Do not book flights around a date you read on a random website. When you are ready to plan, tell the koach your travel window and the koach will confirm the current schedule with the Ga Traditional Council and the Ghana Tourism Authority, and line your days up with the right town's celebration. That is exactly the kind of thing the koach is here to get right for you.

It also happens to be smart timing. August through October is Ghana's richest festival stretch, and it is when the diaspora homecoming crowd starts arriving. Homowo is a wonderful first taste of that season, right in the capital, before you head off to the castles and the north.
How to experience it with respect
Homowo is a sacred harvest rite as much as it is a street party, so the koach asks you to come as a warm guest, not a spectator behind a lens.

x: Go with a local guide or a Ga host. The festival has layers, sacred moments, family moments, public moments, and a good local guide knows which is which and where a visitor is genuinely welcome. The koach can put you with the right one.

Ask before you photograph. The processions and the dancing are yours to enjoy and film. The ritual sprinkling and the shrines are more sensitive. When in doubt, ask, or simply lower the camera and watch.
Dress the part. White is the festive colour, especially around the twins' celebration. Something clean and bright, comfortable shoes, and a hat for the August sun between the showers.
Eat the kpokpoi. If you are offered a bowl in a family compound, that is an honour. Accept it, eat with your right hand, and say oyiwaladonn, thank you, in Ga. You will make a friend for life.
Bring cash and patience. The old quarters get gloriously crowded on the main days. Move slowly, keep your valuables close, and let the day unfold at its own pace.

body.x: Pair it with the rest of Accra

The beauty of a festival in the capital is that everything else is right there. Build a few ordinary Accra days around your Homowo day: the markets and the seafront of Jamestown, the food and nightlife of Osu, a lazy afternoon up in the cool hills at Aburi. The koach has already written you the guides to a lot of this, from what your first days in Accra should feel like to an easy day trip up to the Aburi gardens. Slot Homowo in the middle and you have a week that swings from garden calm to street thunder and back.

And because this is green season, remember the koach's standing advice: travel in the low season on purpose. August in Accra is warm, occasionally wet, and far less crowded than December, and the festival goes ahead rain or shine. A short downpour has never stopped a Ga drummer.
The bigger picture

The koach has shown you Ghana's heavy history at the coast and its wild spaces up north. Homowo is something else again: a city celebrating itself, its harvest, its ancestors, its twins, its long memory of hunger beaten. It is proof that the best of Ghana is not only in the guidebook sites but in a Jamestown lane on an August Saturday, drums going, kpokpoi on the ground, everyone home.

If you want your first trip to Ghana to include one day where you are not a tourist looking at the past but a guest inside the living present, ask the koach to build your visit around Homowo. Tell the koach your dates. The koach will find the town, the guide, the family table, and the drums.
Come hoot at hunger with us.

title: Where the river meets the sea: a two-water weekend at Ada Foah
excerpt: The koach has sent you to castles, courts, and savanna. This week we go somewhere gentler: the sandbar at Ada Foah, where the Volta River pours into the Atlantic and you can stand with calm lagoon water on one side and ocean surf on the other. Here is how to plan a slow green-season weekend by the estuary, boat trips and all.
heroAlt: The Ada Foah sandbar at golden morning light, a thin palm-lined spit of white sand with the calm Volta River lagoon on one side and Atlantic surf breaking on the other, a wooden pirogue drawn up on the sand
author: TripKoach

body.x: Akwaaba. Last week the koach handed you a date, the first of August on the Cape Coast. This week the koach hands you water. Two kinds of it, meeting in one place.

Drive a couple of hours east of Accra and the coast changes. The traffic thins, the palms lean in, and the land runs out into a long finger of white sand where the Volta River finally reaches the Atlantic Ocean after its journey down from the north. This is Ada Foah, and the koach thinks it is the easiest good weekend in the whole country. Calm river water on one side, ocean waves on the other, a sandbar in between, and very little you are obliged to do. After five weeks of heritage and hiking, that is the point.
Let's plan it.
The two-water thing
Most beaches give you one body of water. Ada gives you two, and the space between them is the whole draw.

On one side is the estuary, the wide, brackish, slow water where the Volta spreads out and empties into the sea. It is calm, it is warm, and it is dotted with little estuary islands you can reach only by boat. On the other side is the open Atlantic, with real surf and a long empty beach. Between the two lies a sandbar, a low spit of palm and sand, and standing on it with a paddle in one hand you can look left at flat lagoon water and right at breaking waves. The koach has watched first-timers spend twenty minutes just turning their head back and forth.

Because the river is calm, the water sports here are the gentle kind. Kayaking and canoeing on the lagoon side, boat cruises out to the islands, fishing with the local boatmen, and swimming where the water is flat. The ocean side is for walking and watching the waves, not for strong swimmers to get brave. Respect the Atlantic. It has a pull.
A word on the season

You are reading this in July, which is green season on the southern coast, and the koach will be honest with you the way the koach always is. Ada gets its heaviest rain from June into September, so you are not booking a guaranteed week of blue sky. What you are booking is the quiet version of Ada: soft skies, a river running full, the lodges half empty, and prices that are kinder than they are in the December rush. The rain here tends to come in short bursts and then clear, and the estuary is beautiful under cloud. The koach wrote a whole case for green-season travel a few weeks back, and Ada is exactly the kind of place that argument was built for. Bring a light rain layer, keep your plans loose, and let the weather do what it does.
Getting there

By road from Accra. Ada Foah sits about 110 kilometres east of the capital, and the drive is a straight, easy run of roughly two to two and a half hours on the Accra to Aflao road, out through Tema and Prampram to the Ada junction, then down to the water. It is one of the more relaxed road trips out of Accra, no mountains, no switchbacks, just the coast rolling by. A private hire car or a comfortable transfer is the simplest way; leave the city mid-morning and you are dipping your feet in by lunch.

Where to sleep. The riverside is lined with holiday chalets and a handful of small eco-lodges and beach camps, ranging from rustic sandbar huts you reach by boat to tidier resorts back in town with pools and proper kitchens. Book ahead even in the low season, because Ada is Accra's favourite weekend escape and the good spots fill on Fridays. The koach keeps a shortlist for guests and will match you to the right one for your budget and your appetite for roughing it. Some are barefoot-simple, some are air-conditioned; tell the koach which you are.
The koach's weekend plan
Built for a Friday afternoon arrival and a Sunday departure, at the koach's favourite speed, which is slow.
Friday: arrive and do nothing

Drive down after lunch, drop your bags, and let the weekend start the way an Ada weekend should, with your feet up and the river going pink at sunset. Eat fresh grilled tilapia or the day's catch, listen to the water, and turn in early. You did not come here to rush.
Saturday: the estuary and the islands

This is your big day on the water. Take a morning boat cruise out onto the estuary, weaving between the low green islands to the mouth where the river actually meets the sea. Ask the boatman to land you on the sandbar so you can walk the spit, swim on the calm side, and stand at the meeting of the two waters. Back on the lagoon in the afternoon, take a kayak out for an hour, or simply find a hammock. In the evening the local drumming often starts up somewhere along the shore, and you follow your ears.
Sunday: salt, birds, and a slow road home

Before you drive back, look inland to the Songor Lagoon, the vast wetland behind Ada that has been a salt-making ground for centuries and is a protected Ramsar site rich with birdlife. A short guided visit shows you the shimmering salt pans and, if you are lucky with the light, wading birds by the hundred. Then take an easy breakfast, let the weekend settle, and roll back into Accra by the afternoon, sandy and slow and better for it.
A little history on the sand

Ada is not only a beach. Down near the estuary stand the eroded remains of Fort Kongenstein, built by Danish traders in 1783 and, like the great castles further west, tied into the transatlantic slave trade before it passed to the British in 1850. The sea has been reclaiming it for generations, and today only fragments remain, half in the water. It is a quiet, sobering stop, a reminder that this gentle coast carries the same heavy history as the Cape Coast the koach walked you through earlier this year. Ask a local guide to point out what is left.
If you can time it: Asafotufiami

Here is the koach's planning tip for the weeks ahead. Every year in the first week of August, the chiefs and people of Ada throw one of the liveliest festivals on the Greater Accra calendar: Asafotufiami, the war festival. The name means the divisional firing of musketry, and that is exactly what you get, warriors in traditional dress firing muskets, a grand durbar of chiefs in full colour, drumming, and a re-enactment of the battles through which the Ada people won this stretch of coast. In 2026 the celebration opens in early August, and the Ada Traditional Council has said this year's edition will launch the milestone ninetieth festival. If you can stretch your Ada weekend into the first week of August, you get the estuary and the pageantry in one trip. Confirm the exact dates with the Ada Traditional Council or the Ghana Tourism Authority closer to the time, because the programme shifts a little year to year.
Practical koach notes

x: Pack for two waters and a little rain. Swimwear, a hat, sunscreen, reef-friendly if you have it, and a light rain shell for the green-season showers. Sandals you do not mind getting wet.
Bring cash in cedis. Ada is a small town and the boat trips, drinks, and local kitchens run on cash. Pull cedis in Accra before you leave; do not count on an ATM at the sandbar.
Agree the boat price first. Settle the fare with your boatman before you push off, and tip well for a good trip. The estuary boatmen know these waters and the islands better than any map.
Mind the ocean side. The Atlantic here has a strong pull and no lifeguards. Swim on the calm lagoon side and enjoy the surf side with your feet, not your whole body.

Turtles have a season, and it is not now. Ada's beaches host nesting sea turtles, but the season runs roughly November to March. Come in those months if the turtles are why you are here; in July, come for the water and the quiet.
Green-season plans stay loose. A short downpour is not a ruined day here. Build in slack, keep the boat trip flexible, and let the weather clear itself, which it usually does.

body.x: The bigger picture

The koach has spent the last month and more showing you Ghana's big, heavy, unforgettable places, the dungeons at Cape Coast, the Asante court at Kumasi, the elephants at Mole. Ada is the country in a different key. It is where Accra goes to breathe, where a whole river lays down its long journey and hands itself to the sea, and where the only real decision is whether to kayak now or nap first.

If your first trip to Ghana has been all history and altitude, or if you have just landed and want to know what your first days in Accra should feel like, let Ada be the soft landing. Two waters, one sandbar, a boat, and a weekend with nothing you have to do.
Book the Friday. Pack light. The koach has the rest.

title: Emancipation Day on the Cape Coast: planning a homecoming weekend for August 1
excerpt: For five weeks the koach has sent you walking, hiking, and tracking elephants. This week we slow down and look at the calendar, because the most moving date in Ghana's tourism year is coming. Here is how to plan an Emancipation Day weekend on the Cape Coast, from Reverential Night at the castle to the slave river at Assin Manso.
heroAlt: A candlelight vigil at dusk outside the white walls of Cape Coast Castle, a crowd dressed in white holding small flames, the Gulf of Guinea dark behind the ramparts, warm low light on the stone
author: TripKoach

body.x: Akwaaba. For five Mondays running the koach has handed you a place: the Wli waterfalls, the Asante court at Kumasi, the savanna and the elephants up at Mole. This week the koach hands you a date instead.

On the first of August, Ghana marks Emancipation Day, and the centre of it is the Cape Coast. It is not a beach weekend and it is not a checklist of sights. It is the single most powerful few days on the country's calendar, the days when the diaspora comes home to the very ground their ancestors were taken from, and the nation stops to remember out loud. If you are thinking about a heritage trip this year, this is the weekend to build it around, and the koach wants you planning now while the good rooms in Cape Coast are still open.
Let's walk through it.
What Emancipation Day actually is

The first of August is the anniversary of the 1834 abolition of slavery across the British Empire. Caribbean nations have marked it for generations. In 1998 Ghana became the first African country to formally adopt the observance and to invite the global African family to keep it on home soil, on the very coast the transatlantic trade ran through. It has been an anchor of Ghana's heritage tourism ever since, and it sits inside the wider Beyond the Return diaspora movement that has been bringing record numbers of visitors through Accra's Kotoka airport.

So this is not a festival you watch. It is a commemoration you take part in. The mood is solemn, proud, and communal, somewhere between a memorial, a family reunion, and a national durbar. People wear white. People weep and then they dance. The koach has seen first-time visitors arrive as tourists and leave as something closer to family.
The shape of the weekend

The official programme shifts a little year to year, and the Ghana Tourism Authority publishes the final schedule closer to the date, but the spine of it has held for years. Here is the shape the koach plans around.
July 31, evening: Reverential Night at Cape Coast Castle

The vigil is the emotional heart of it. On the night of the thirty-first, the crowd gathers at Cape Coast Castle dressed in white for Reverential Night, a candlelight procession and vigil for the millions who died in the dungeons and on the crossing. There are drums, libation, readings, and a long, quiet wait by the sea wall. Standing in the lower courtyard at night, with the surf hitting the rocks below the Door of No Return, is not something the koach can describe for you. You have to be in it.
Wear white. Bring a light layer for the sea breeze. Arrive early, because the courtyard fills.
August 1, morning: the slave river at Assin Manso

The first of August moves inland, about forty minutes north of Cape Coast on the road towards Kumasi, to Assin Manso. This is the site of the Donko Nsuo, the slave river, where captives marched down from the north were given a last bath before the final walk to the coastal dungeons. Beside it lies the Ancestral Burial Ground, where in 1998 the remains of two returnees, one from the United States and one from Jamaica, were reburied in Ghanaian soil in a ceremony that gave the whole observance its meaning.

The morning at Assin Manso brings a Grand Durbar of chiefs in full regalia, drumming, libation at the river, and a wreath-laying at the graves. Many diaspora visitors take their own quiet moment at the water. It is open, it is welcoming, and it asks nothing of you but presence.
August 1, afternoon: back to the coast and the dungeons

The day usually closes back on the coast with wreath-laying and ceremonies at Cape Coast Castle and, thirteen kilometres west, Elmina Castle, the oldest European building south of the Sahara. If you have never walked the dungeons and stood at the Door of No Return in daylight, do it now, with a guide, slowly. The koach wrote a fuller field guide to both castles a few weeks back, and everything in it still holds for this weekend. Read it before you come so the history is already in you when you arrive.
The koach's three-day plan
Built for a Friday arrival in Cape Coast and a Sunday departure, with Emancipation Day itself on the Saturday in 2026.
Getting there

By road from Accra. Cape Coast sits about 145 km west of the capital on the N1 coastal highway, roughly two and a half to three hours depending on the Kasoa stretch. A private transfer or a comfortable trotro-free hire car is the easy option. Leave Accra in the morning to dodge the worst of the traffic out of the city.

Where to sleep. Cape Coast and Elmina have a real spread of guesthouses and beach hotels, and Emancipation week is their busiest of the year, so book now, not in July. Base yourself in or near Cape Coast town so you are minutes from the castle for the night vigil.
Day one, Friday: settle in, see the castle by day

Arrive, drop your bags, and take an afternoon guided tour of Cape Coast Castle while it is calm. The on-site museum lays out the history of the trade and of Ghana's independence, and walking the dungeons in daylight, before the emotion of the vigil, lets you absorb the facts first. Eat fresh-grilled fish by the water in the evening and turn in early.
Day two, Saturday: Assin Manso, then Reverential build-up

Drive up to Assin Manso in the morning for the durbar and the slave river. Take your time at the Donko Nsuo and the Ancestral Burial Ground. Back in Cape Coast by mid-afternoon, rest, change into white, and join Reverential Night at the castle after dark. This is the centre of the whole trip. Give it the evening.
Day three, Sunday: Elmina, and a slow road home

Spend the morning at Elmina Castle and the fishing harbour below it, where the painted pirogues stack up against the old Portuguese walls in a scene that has not really changed in centuries. Take a quiet breakfast, let the weekend settle, and drive back to Accra in the afternoon.
Practical koach notes

x: Book accommodation now. Emancipation week is the single busiest stretch of the year for Cape Coast and Elmina. June planning gets you a room. July planning gets you a long drive back to Accra each night.
Wear white for the vigil. It is the expected dress for Reverential Night and it matters. A simple white shirt and trousers or a white dress is plenty.

Confirm the official programme. The Ghana Tourism Authority and the Ministry of Tourism release the finalised dates and venues each year. Check the official schedule a week or two out, because individual events can shift by a day.
Bring cash in cedis. Cape Coast has ATMs but the queues swell during the week. Pull cedis in Accra before you leave.
Come with respect, not just a camera. Ask before photographing people at the durbar or in their grief. This is a commemoration, and the dignity of it is the point.

PANAFEST years. Emancipation Day has a biennial sister, PANAFEST, the Pan-African Historical Theatre Festival, which fills the surrounding weeks with performances, colloquia, and a durbar when it falls. Check the GTA calendar to see whether your year is a PANAFEST year, and if it is, give yourself extra days.
Health and sun. The coast is hot and humid in August even under cloud. Water, a hat, and sunscreen. The vigil aside, you are outdoors a lot.

body.x: The bigger picture

The koach has spent five weeks showing you that Ghana is many countries stitched into one: the rainforest east, the Asante heartland, the savanna north. Emancipation Day is the week that shows you the other thing about this country, the reason so many travellers describe Ghana not as a place they visited but as a place that claimed them.

You can come to the Cape Coast any week of the year and the castles will be there, white and terrible and beautiful against the sea. But for these few days at the start of August, you do not stand in front of the history alone. You stand in a crowd dressed in white, holding a candle, with the ocean in the dark and the drums starting up, and the past is not behind glass. It is right there with you, and so is everybody else who came home to meet it.
Plan the rooms now. Pack the white shirt. The koach has the rest.

title: Mole and Larabanga: a savanna weekend with elephants and West Africa's oldest mosque
excerpt: Last week the koach sent you to the Asante court. This week we head north into the Guinea savanna, where Africa's oldest game reserve puts you on foot with elephants and a 600-year-old adobe mosque sits ten minutes down the road. A practical green-season plan.
heroAlt: Two African savanna elephants drinking at a waterhole beneath a broad acacia, dry golden grass stretching out behind them, low warm sunlight, birds in flight in the sky to the right
author: TripKoach

body.x: Akwaaba. Last week the koach took you to Manhyia in Kumasi. This week we go further north and further out, into the Guinea savanna of the Savannah Region, because there is one Ghana experience the koach hears about more than any other from first-time visitors, and we have not written it up yet.

The pitch is short. Mole National Park is the oldest and largest protected area in Ghana, roughly 4,840 square kilometres of bush, river, and acacia, with around 800 African savanna elephants, antelope, baboons, warthogs, and birds the koach cannot keep up with. You can walk in it. Not in a vehicle, on your own two feet, with an armed ranger in front of you, ten or twenty metres from a feeding elephant. There is no charge for the adrenaline.

Ten minutes down the laterite road sits Larabanga, a small village built around what the locals call the Mecca of West Africa, an adobe mosque that has been standing in the same Sudano-Sahelian shape since 1421. Same trip, same weekend.
The koach has been saving this one. Let's plan it.
Why Mole, why now
Three reasons line up cleanly.

The wildlife is genuinely there. Estimates for the elephant herd sit above 800, and you will see at least a small group on a single morning walk if you go to the waterhole below Mole Motel. Kob, waterbuck, bushbuck, warthog, and baboons are routine. Hippos pool in the rivers. Lions still appear in the park records but sightings are rare. Mole has been protected since 1971 and the rangers know the ground.

June is green season, which has trade-offs in your favour. The savanna is lush, the prices are off-peak, and the lodges are quiet. You will not get the dry-season concentration of animals around dwindling waterholes that you get from January to April, but you will get cooler mornings, dramatic skies, baby animals, and almost no crowds. The koach reads it as the calm, cheap shoulder of a destination that gets busy in winter.

The northern road keeps getting easier. The asphalt from Tamale through Damongo to Mole is in good shape. Africa World Airlines and Passion Air run multiple daily flights from Accra to Tamale. If you have three days, you can do it without a car. If you have four, you can drive and see the Black Volta on the way.
The koach's three-day plan
This is built for a Friday evening fly-in from Accra and a Sunday evening fly-back, which is the most realistic shape for a working week.
Getting there

By air to Tamale, then road. Tamale Airport is the gateway. Flight is roughly 60 to 75 minutes. From the airport, a chartered taxi or arranged transfer to Mole is around 146 km on the N10 through Fufulso Junction and Damongo. Plan three hours including a coffee stop. A standard sedan handles the road. Book the transfer ahead of time, not on arrival.

By road from Accra. This is roughly 620 km via Kumasi, Kintampo, Tamale, and Damongo. Two driving days if you want to enjoy it, with a Kintampo or Tamale overnight. The koach only recommends the drive if you actually want to see the country in between. The Kintampo Waterfalls are worth a stretch-stop.
By coach. STC runs Accra to Tamale overnight. From Tamale the shared taxis to Damongo, then on to Mole, are doable but slow. Budget travellers do it. First-timers should fly.
Day one: arrive at Mole, settle, sunset walk

Base inside the park or right at the gate. There are two well-known options. Zaina Lodge is the upmarket choice, an eco-lodge built on the escarpment with chalets looking down on the waterhole. Mole Motel is the original government-run hotel with a swimming pool that has the best view in Ghana, and rooms that are clean and basic. Either way, you wake up on the cliff above the elephants.

Evening walking safari. Most lodges run two ranger-guided walks a day, an early morning one starting around 6:30 AM and a late afternoon one around 3:30 PM. The walk is around two hours, the pace is slow, and the ranger carries a rifle for the worst case. He will explain tracks, dung age, the alarm calls of baboons, and the wind direction you need to keep the elephants relaxed. Wear closed shoes. Long trousers. No bright colours. Listen more than you talk.
Day two: morning game drive, afternoon Larabanga

Morning game drive. Vehicles are open-sided 4x4s arranged through the park or your lodge. This is where you cover ground the walks cannot reach, get closer to herds at the more distant waterholes, and meet the antelope species that hang back from the main area. Two and a half hours, leave at first light, take a warm layer for the open back. The koach's tip: ask the driver to detour past Samole and Konkori if water is high.
Lunch back at base. Then Larabanga.

Larabanga Mosque. A ten-minute drive from the park gate. The mosque is small, four conical adobe towers, walls reinforced with timber pegs, founded in 1421 according to oral tradition and continuously maintained. It is listed by the World Monuments Fund as a Most Endangered Site, and the village runs a small visitor centre next door. Pay the modest entry fee at the visitor centre, take a guide, and respect the rules: non-Muslim visitors do not enter the prayer hall, modest dress is expected, women cover heads, photos of the exterior are usually fine but ask first. The mystic stone is still there beside the mosque, and the guide will tell you the dream story. The koach's read: this is one of the most quietly remarkable buildings in West Africa, and you stand in front of it with no crowd and no queue.
Back to the lodge for the second walking safari. A different ranger sees different things. Do it twice if the legs cooperate.
Day three: dawn at the waterhole, slow drive back

Sunrise on the escarpment. Mole Motel's terrace and Zaina's deck both look straight down onto the main waterhole. Get there with coffee at 5:45 AM. You will almost certainly see elephants drinking and bathing in the cool of the morning. This is the koach's favourite hour in Ghana, no exaggeration.

Slow drive back to Tamale for the afternoon flight. Leave Mole by 11 AM. Stop at Fufulso for the junction snacks. If your flight is late enough, a quick swing through central Tamale lets you eat at one of the city's chop bars and walk past the Central Mosque on the way to the airport. Sunday flights to Accra are usually wide open.
Practical koach notes

x: Park entry and walking safari fees: payable in cedis at the park gate, with separate rates for Ghanaian and non-resident visitors. Confirm current prices with your lodge before you arrive.
Cash: Damongo has ATMs that work most of the time, but treat them as a backup. Pull cedis in Tamale or before you fly.

What to pack: closed shoes for the walks, long lightweight trousers, a wide-brim hat, a rain shell for green-season showers, mosquito repellent with DEET, a head covering for Larabanga, and binoculars if you have them.
Health: Northern Ghana is a malaria zone. Take your prophylaxis. Lodges have nets. Drink bottled or filtered water.
Phones and signal: MTN works at both lodges. Data is patchy on the walks. Tell someone at home your schedule before you go off-grid.
Photographing people: ask before you take a portrait in Larabanga village. Tip the guide.
Festival overlap: if your trip lands near a Damba or Bugum festival in Tamale, plan a buffer day. Northern festivals are worth a detour, not a missed flight.

body.x: The bigger picture

Two weeks ago the koach sent you to the Wli waterfalls in the east. Last week to the Asante court in Kumasi. This week to the savanna and the adobe mosque in the north. The thing the koach wants you to feel by the end of this run of posts is that Ghana is not one trip, it is a region with four or five completely different countries inside it, and the only reason most visitors miss the north is that nobody told them how easy it is to get there now.

Mole has been on the list since 1971. The mosque has been on it since 1421. The flights, the road, and the lodges are ready. The elephants do not know it is green season. They just want the waterhole.
Pack the closed shoes. The koach has the rest.

title: Kumasi in a weekend: Manhyia, Kejetia, and timing it around Akwasidae
excerpt: The Asante capital is having a moment. Returned royal regalia at Manhyia, a packed Akwasidae calendar this summer, and the loudest, friendliest market in West Africa. The koach's two-day Kumasi plan, with the booking hook for Sunday 19 July.
heroAlt: The ornate front gate of Manhyia Palace in Kumasi at midday, the Asante royal coat of arms picked out in gold above deep ochre walls, a black star and ceremonial sword bearer crest carved into the lintel, mango trees framing the empty courtyard before a durbar
author: TripKoach

body.x: Akwaaba. Last week the koach sent you east to Wli. This week we go north and inland, to the Asante capital, because Kumasi is having a year and the timing window for the next big festival is short.

Here is the short version. Manhyia Palace reopened its museum in 2024 with 32 pieces of Asante royal regalia that the British Museum and the Victoria and Albert Museum loaned back for the first time in over a century. The Asantehene's Silver Jubilee year set off a wave of cultural programming that is still rolling. And the next Akwasidae, the royal durbar that happens every six weeks on a Sunday at Manhyia, lands on Sunday 19 July 2026. If you have been waiting for a reason to plan a Kumasi trip, the koach has been waiting to write this post for you.
Pack a small bag. Bring a head covering. We are going to court.
Why Kumasi, why right now
Three things are stacked in your favour at the same time.

The regalia is home, at least for now. When Manhyia Palace Museum reopened in May 2024 as part of Otumfuo Osei Tutu II's Silver Jubilee, it did so with the Asante Regalia Homecoming Exhibition, a long term loan of golden ornaments, ceremonial swords, and the kind of objects that were taken in the 1874 sack of Kumasi and never returned. You can stand in front of them now. The Otumfuo has been clear that more negotiations with foreign museums are ongoing. Go while the loan is live.

Akwasidae is a real living festival, not a reenactment. It happens on a Sunday every 42 days on the Akan calendar, with the Asantehene receiving chiefs, linguists, sword bearers, and umbrella carriers in full regalia at Manhyia. Visitors are welcome. The next one in the window the koach is writing for is Sunday 19 July 2026, then Sunday 30 August 2026. You can build a weekend around either.

The Ghana Tourism Marketplace went live on 12 May 2026. The country is finally putting domestic experiences in one bookable place, and the Ashanti Region is one of the headline destinations on it. Roads from Accra are passable through green season, and the city itself is in cool, slightly damp June form, which is the koach's favourite Kumasi weather.
The koach's two-day Kumasi plan
This works as a Friday evening fly in, Sunday evening fly out, or as a road trip if you have the stamina for the N6.
Getting there

By road from Accra. It is roughly 250 km on the N6 through Nsawam, Nkawkaw, and Konongo. Plan four to five hours in good traffic, longer on Fridays after 3 PM. Leave Accra by 6 AM if you want to arrive in Kumasi for a real lunch. The Linda Dor stop at Bunso Junction is the koach's standing recommendation for jollof and toilets.

By air. Africa World Airlines and Passion Air fly Accra to Kumasi multiple times daily out of Terminal 2. The hop is 45 minutes in the air. From Kumasi Airport to the city centre is a 15 minute drive on a Sunday morning.

By coach. STC and VIP run Accra to Kumasi from Tudu and the new VVIP terminal in Circle. Reserve a seat the day before. The night coach is cheaper. The day coach is safer if you are a first-time visitor.
Day one: settle in, see the city

Base in Adum, Asokwa, or Ahodwo. Adum puts you walking distance to Kejetia and Manhyia. Asokwa is closer to the airport and the malls. Ahodwo gives you the quietest sleep. Lancaster Kumasi City Hotel, Royal Lamerta, and Golden Bean are the reliable mid-range picks the koach hears repeat business about.

Afternoon at Manhyia Palace Museum. Entry is around GHS 50 for non-Ghanaian visitors and less for Ghanaians, paid at the gate. Tours are guided and run roughly hourly. The Homecoming Exhibition is the headline. The older galleries show the wax figures of Asantehenes past, the gold weights and stools, and the original audience room used by Prempeh I and Prempeh II. Allow ninety minutes minimum. Take your shoes off where asked, and put your phone away when the guide says so.

Late afternoon at the Centre for National Culture. A short drive from Manhyia, the Cultural Centre is set in shady grounds with the Prempeh II Jubilee Museum, craft workshops, and a small restaurant. This is where the koach sends people who want to watch a kente loom going in real time without making the trip to Bonwire. Buy small things here. Save the big spending for the village.

Dinner. Vic Baboo's Café for the koach's classic comfort plate. Chopstix or Calbar for Chinese done well. For something fully local, ask for the kontomire stew with omotuo at any small chop bar in Adum and tip the cook.
Day two: the village, the market, and Akwasidae if you timed it right

If your Sunday is an Akwasidae Sunday (19 July or 30 August 2026): go to Manhyia first. The durbar starts in the morning. Arrive by 9 AM, dress respectfully, women cover shoulders, men in long trousers, no red or black for happy festivals. You do not need a ticket to the public courtyard. Move quietly. Stand when the Asantehene enters. Photos are usually allowed but follow the linguist's signals. You will see the gold umbrellas, hear the fontomfrom drums, and watch a court that has been in continuous operation since the seventeenth century. The koach has not found a better cultural hour in West Africa.
If your Sunday is not Akwasidae: go to the villages instead.

x: Bonwire, 18 km northeast of Kumasi. This is where Asante kente is woven. You will see strip looms set up in courtyards, weavers explaining the pattern names, and finished cloth for sale at workshop prices instead of market markup. Ask for the patterns by name. Adweneasa, Sika Futuro, Oyokoman, all have stories. The koach's standing rule: buy from the weaver, not the middle man.

Ntonso, 20 km north on the Mampong road. Adinkra stamping. You can have a cloth printed for you while you watch, using the carved calabash stamps and the dark dye made from bark. Half day, low cost, a real souvenir.
Ahwiaa, on the way to Mampong. Wood carving. Stools, masks, and walking sticks made in front of you. Bring cash.

body.x: Lunch back in town, then Kejetia. Kejetia is West Africa's largest open-air market, roughly ten thousand stalls under one giant roof and the spillover streets around it. It is loud, hot, and the koach's favourite kind of overwhelming. Go with a guide for your first time, give yourself two hours minimum, and head for the cloth section near the front for the cleanest introduction. Pickpockets are real. Wear your bag in front. Bargain in cedis, not dollars.

Evening at Lake Bosomtwe, if you have a third day. An hour southeast of Kumasi, Ghana's only natural lake sits inside a crater the locals consider sacred. A few small lodges on the shore. Quiet swim, fresh tilapia, and a good place to decompress before the drive back.
Practical koach notes

x: Cash: carry cedis in small notes for the museum, the village workshops, and Kejetia. ATMs are easy in Adum and at the malls.
What to wear: modest, light, breathable. Bring a covering for Manhyia. A rain shell for late afternoon showers in June.
Photos at Manhyia: allowed in most galleries, restricted in the audience room and during certain durbar moments. Follow the guide. Do not film children without asking.
Language: Twi is the working language. Maakye for good morning, medaase for thank you, and yoo to acknowledge. People will warm up fast.
Festival etiquette: no red or black at Akwasidae, no walking in front of the Asantehene, no shouting at the drummers. Tip linguists and guides discreetly.
Drive plan back to Accra: leave Kumasi by 2 PM on Sunday. The N6 chokes after 5 PM on Sunday evenings near Nsawam.

body.x: The bigger picture

The koach reads the Kumasi moment simply. The country is investing in heritage tourism the way it invested in Cape Coast in the 2010s, the regalia is back at Manhyia for the first time in living memory, and the Asantehene's Silver Jubilee programming has put the city back on the diaspora travel map. The Ghana Tourism Authority is leaning in. The Tourism Marketplace is making bookings easier. The infrastructure is moving in your favour.
Go before everyone else figures it out. Then come home for jollof.

title: Wli Falls: the Volta weekend that earns the drive
excerpt: Five hours northeast of Accra, West Africa's tallest waterfall is at its loudest, the fruit bats are out at dusk, and the Volta hills are doing their green season thing. Here is the koach's two-day plan for Wli.
heroAlt: The lower Wli Falls plunging down a tall cliff face in Ghana's Volta Region, white water against dark wet rock, lush green forest framing the pool below
author: TripKoach

body.x: Akwaaba. If Aburi felt like cheating because it was so close to Accra, this week we are going the other way. The koach is sending you east, up the Volta Region, to the foot of a 80 metre cliff where West Africa's tallest waterfall is currently roaring at peak flow, and a few thousand fruit bats are clinging to the wet rock waiting for sunset.
Pack a small bag. This one earns a weekend.
Why Wli, why right now

Wli Falls sits just outside Hohoe in the Volta Region, tucked into the Agumatsa Wildlife Sanctuary and fed by a stream that actually starts across the border in Yikpa, Togo. It is the tallest waterfall in Ghana and in all of West Africa, and from April through October it is at full volume. We are sitting in the middle of that window. You can hear the lower falls before you see them. You can feel the spray on your face from the viewing pool. By August the trail gets muddier and the drive longer, so the koach picks June for the sweet spot.

The other reason to go now is policy weather. President Mahama has appointed both the Tourism Minister and the Roads and Highways Minister from the Volta Region, and the Ghana Tourism Authority is leaning hard into Volta as the next big domestic story after Cape Coast. Roads are getting touched up. Signage is going in. The infrastructure is moving in your favour.
The koach's two-day Wli plan
Day one: drive up, settle in

Leave Accra Saturday by 6:30 AM. The drive is roughly 230 km and takes four to five hours depending on Aflao Junction traffic. You want to arrive in Hohoe with daylight to spare, so an early roll out of the city is non-negotiable. Stop at Atimpoku for the riverside grilled tilapia and one-man-thousand on the Volta River bridge. It is the koach's favourite first photo of the trip.

Base in Hohoe or Wli village. Hohoe town has the most options, including the steady Matse Hotel and a few newer guesthouses on the Wli road. If you want to wake up inside the sanctuary, book Wli Water Heights Hotel right at the village. It is simple, the staff are warm, and you are a fifteen minute walk from the visitor centre.

Afternoon at the visitor centre. Pay your gate fee at the booth, around GHS 20 to 30 per person, sign the book, and pick up a community guide. Guides are required for the upper falls and worth it for the lower trail too. They know which butterflies are in season and where the bats are quietest.
Day two: the falls, both of them if you can

Lower falls at sunrise. The trail to the lower falls is a 2.2 km flat walk that crosses the Agumatsa stream on small wooden bridges. Plan for 45 minutes in, longer if you stop for photos of the swallowtails. The reward is a viewing pool right at the foot of the cliff, the water hitting hard enough to throw cool mist over the whole clearing. Look up. Those dark patches on the rock face are not stains. They are thousands of straw coloured fruit bats, and at dusk they pour off the cliff in a single long ribbon. Even if you only do the lower trail, the koach promises you have not seen Ghana like this.

Upper falls for the stubborn. The upper trail is a different animal. Four hours round trip, a stiff climb up the ridge, slick switchbacks in places, and a difficulty rating that locals do not exaggerate. Wear real shoes. Take two litres of water. The reward at the top is a much taller, much quieter cascade with almost nobody else around. If your knees are saying no, the lower trail is plenty.
Lunch in Wli village. Banku and grilled tilapia at one of the village spots. Ask for the goat light soup if it is on. The koach also rates the akple at the small place opposite the chief's palace.

Optional add on: Tafi Atome monkey sanctuary. Forty minutes south of Wli, the mona monkeys come down to eat bananas from your hand. Small entry fee, big payoff for kids and first-time visitors. If you have a Sunday afternoon to spare before driving back, this is the koach's pick to bolt onto the trip.

Drive back to Accra Sunday evening. Aim to leave Hohoe by 3 PM at the latest. Sunday traffic into Accra from the east starts biting around Adomi Bridge after 6 PM, and you want to be inside the city before it does.
Practical koach notes

x: Cash: bring small cedi notes for the gate, the guide tip, and village lunches. ATMs are easier to find in Hohoe than in Wli itself.

What to wear: lightweight long sleeves and trousers for the lower trail because the canopy is humid and the mosquitoes wake up at dusk. Real hiking shoes if you are doing the upper falls. A rain shell does not hurt.
Guide tip: GHS 50 to 100 per group is the going koach rate for the lower falls. Double it if they take you upper.
Cell signal: patchy in the sanctuary, fine in Hohoe. Tell someone your plan before you start the upper trail.

Getting there without a car: STC and VIP coaches run Accra to Hohoe daily from Tudu and the new VVIP terminal. From Hohoe a shared taxi to Wli village is around GHS 15. It is doable without a private vehicle.

body.x: A small note on the bigger picture

Ghana has been quietly stacking momentum this year. The Ghana Tourism Marketplace platform went live on 12 May 2026 to put domestic experiences in one bookable place, and the country leaned hard into intra-African travel and MICE growth at WTM Africa 2026 last month. The Volta push is part of that same story. The koach reads it simply: spots like Wli that used to need a guidebook and a local cousin are getting easier to plan, and the timing has never been better to put them on your list.
Go before everyone else figures it out. Then come home for jollof.

title: Up the ridge: the Aburi day trip when Accra gets warm
excerpt: An hour out of Accra, the air drops a few degrees, the palms close in overhead, and a cocoa tree from 1879 is still quietly making history. Here is the koach plan for one easy day on the Akuapem ridge.
heroAlt: The Royal Palm Avenue at Aburi Botanical Gardens in soft morning light, two tall columns of palms framing a damp green pathway up the Akuapem ridge in eastern Ghana
author: TripKoach

body.x: Akwaaba. If you have given Accra a fair few days and your phone is starting to feel slippery in the heat, this is the koach's favourite escape valve: head up the Akuapem ridge to Aburi, lose the city below the cloud line, and be back home for jollof by sunset. One hour out, one hour back, and a botanical garden that has been quietly holding its corner of Ghana's history since 1875.
Here is how to do it without the guesswork.
Why Aburi, why now

June in Accra is sticky. The rains have arrived, the humidity is doing its thing, and the city is alive but loud. Aburi sits about 400 metres above sea level on the Akuapem ridge in the Eastern Region. You feel the temperature drop on the climb up, and by the time you reach the gardens the air is cooler, greener, and a few degrees kinder.

The gardens themselves are 65 hectares of palms, ancient silk cotton trees, medicinal beds and shady lawns laid out by the British in 1875 on the site of an old colonial sanatorium. After independence Ghana kept them and let them mature into one of West Africa's most loved green spaces. Locals come for wedding photos. Schools come for nature walks. The koach comes for the quiet.
The koach's one-day plan
Leave Accra by 7:30 AM. Traffic on the Aburi road is real, especially the climb past Peduase. Early light also gives you the gardens before the school groups arrive.

Stop at the Tetteh Quarshie Cocoa Farm in Mampong. This is the small site where, in 1879, Tetteh Quarshie planted the cocoa seedlings he had carried back from Fernando Po. Every chocolate bar Ghana sells today traces back to those first trees. The visit is short, maybe 30 minutes, but the heritage hit lands.

Royal Palm Avenue at Aburi, on foot. Walk the famous twin row of palms first. It is the photo everyone takes, and it is worth the cliché. Then loop the medicinal gardens, find the "Tree of Life" carving, and sit a while under the silk cotton tree near the western lawns.

Lunch on the ridge. The koach picks Rose Plot Restaurant or one of the open-deck spots along the Aburi-Peduase road for the view. Order grilled tilapia with kenkey, ask for shito on the side, and watch the clouds move across the plains below.
Sunset back down the hill. Time the descent so you cross Peduase as the light goes orange. If you have the stamina, swing through Madina Market on the way back for a bag of fresh tatale or kelewele.
Practical koach notes

x: Gate price: entry to the gardens is modest and posted at the booth. Bring small cedi notes. The Tetteh Quarshie farm has a separate small fee.

Getting there: Uber and Bolt from central Accra usually run around GHS 150 one way, but the return ride is harder to get from the gardens. Either keep your driver waiting (agree the price up front), hop on a tro-tro from Madina Market for GHS 5 to 10, or join a guided day tour and let someone else solve the transport.

What to wear: comfortable shoes for the lawns, a light layer for the ridge breeze (yes, really), and a foldable rain shell. We are in the wet months, and the gardens are at their lushest because of it.
Hours: open daily 8:30 AM to 5:00 PM. Mornings are the koach pick for soft light and quiet paths.
Driving yourself: the road is paved most of the way and the climb is fine in a normal sedan. The last stretch near the gate has some potholes; take it slow.

body.x: A small note on the bigger picture

Ghana is currently in the middle of a tourism push that is finally giving spots like Aburi the attention they deserve. New road works on several inland tourist routes are slated for completion by September 2026, the Ghana Tourism Marketplace launched on 12 May 2026 to put domestic experiences in one bookable place, and the country is leaning into the medical, wellness and intra-African travel angles at WTM Africa 2026. If you have been waiting for Ghana to feel a little easier to navigate, the dust is settling in a good direction.
Aburi is the perfect first taste of that. Half a day off the Accra grid, no flights, no visas, no guesswork. Then jollof, then home.
