title: Cape Coast and Elmina: a koach's guide to the castles
excerpt: How to give Cape Coast and Elmina the day they deserve. Logistics, timing, what to eat, and what to bring with you that is not in your bag.
heroAlt: The seaward walls of Cape Coast Castle rising above the beach with Fante fishing canoes pulled up on the sand in front of it
author: TripKoach

body.x: Akwaaba. If you are planning a Ghana trip, sooner or later somebody will ask you the question. Are you going to Cape Coast.

Most people say yes before they fully understand what they are saying yes to. The castles are not a thing to see. They are a place you walk into one person and walk out of as a slightly different person. This post is the koach's quiet briefing for that day, so you arrive ready and you leave whole.
Cape Coast or Elmina, or both

There are two castles, about fifteen minutes apart on the same coast. Cape Coast Castle is the larger of the two and the one most visitors know by name. Elmina, formally St. George's Castle, is the older one. It was the first European fort built on the West African coast, and the walk through it is in some ways even heavier.

You can do both in one day if you start early. If you only do one, do Cape Coast. If you have a free morning the next day, add Elmina then. Do not try to squeeze them around a lunch break and expect to feel anything but tired.
How to get there from Accra

Cape Coast sits roughly 145 km west of Accra on the N1, and the drive takes 2.5 to 3.5 hours depending on the day. Saturday and Sunday mornings before 8:00 are the fastest run. Friday evenings out of Accra are the slowest. Most koach itineraries pre-book a driver for the full day, because the maths is simple. Round-trip transport, two castle visits, and an unhurried lunch is a 10 to 12 hour day, and you do not want to be hunting for a taxi back to Accra at sunset.

If you want to slow it down, stay overnight in Cape Coast. The town has a string of mid-range guesthouses on the coast road, and you can be at the castle gate when it opens at 09:00, before the heat and the coach groups roll in.
What to do at the castle itself
Take the guided tour. Do not freelance through the rooms. The GMMB guides are local, trained, and they pace the tour so the weight lands without breaking you. Tip them well at the end.

The order of the tour matters. You walk through the male and female dungeons, then through the door of no return, then up to the airy governor's quarters and the chapel built directly over the holding cells. That sequence is the point. It is the architecture of the trade telling its own story.

A koach tip on the dungeons. It is dark, the air is heavy, and the guide speaks softly. Bring a small bottle of water and tuck it in a bag rather than holding it in your hand. You will want both hands free for the walls.
Pair it with Kakum if you have the energy

About 30 minutes inland from Cape Coast is Kakum National Park, with the canopy walkway strung between rainforest treetops. It is a useful counterweight to the castles. High air, green, and a different kind of breath. If you are doing both castles in one day, skip Kakum or save it for the next morning. If you are doing only one castle, Kakum after lunch is a beautiful pairing.
The walkway is cooler and clearer before 11:00. By midday the humidity is real.
What to eat

Cape Coast town does the coast's two big plates well. Fresh grilled tilapia with banku and pepper, and red red, which is bean stew with fried plantain. The kitchens at Oasis Beach Resort and along the castle road are reliable, with sea views. A number of small spots on the main road do honest Ghanaian plates for far less. Ask your driver for the place the drivers eat and trust them.
Eat slow. The day has been heavy. The food is part of putting yourself back together.
What to bring with you that is not in your bag
This is the part most blog posts skip.

You will hear things in the dungeons that do not leave easily. People cry, people go quiet, people get angry. All of that is fine. The koach will not rush you through that part. Bring a friend who knows when to talk and when not to. If you are travelling alone, bring a small notebook for after. Build a soft evening into the itinerary, not a club night.
If you are a returner, the door of no return has another sign on the back of it, facing the ocean. Take a minute with that one. It is the reason a lot of people make this trip.
What the koach handles for you

If TripKoach is planning your trip, the Cape Coast day is one of the days we put the most care into. A driver who has done the route a hundred times. Castle tickets and tour timing sorted. A lunch reservation that holds. A koach on WhatsApp from the moment you set off to the moment you are back at your hotel. We do not script the emotional part of the day. We make sure the logistics never get in the way of it.

title: Your first 24 hours in Accra: the koach's arrival kit
excerpt: SIM, cedis, ride apps, the food that fixes jet lag, and the small moves that set up the rest of your trip. Akwaaba. Here is what to do before you even unpack.
heroAlt: View of an Accra street through the windshield of a shared ride, with billboards, a pickup truck ahead and a Ghana number-plate visible
author: TripKoach

body.x: Akwaaba. The longest flight is done. You step out of Kotoka into warm air, and somewhere between the arrivals hall and the taxi rank you realise the trip just started for real.
Day one is a stack of small decisions, and the right ones make the next ten days easier. Here is the koach's short arrival kit for your first 24 hours in Accra.
1. Sort a local SIM before you leave the airport

MTN, Telecel and AirtelTigo all have desks inside the Kotoka arrivals hall. Bring your passport (Ghana requires SIM registration), pick a tourist data bundle, and walk out paying cedi prices instead of roaming fees. Your ride app, your maps, and WhatsApp home all want a Ghana number.
If the queue is long after a late landing, do not stress. Any MTN or Telecel shop in the city will sort you the next morning, and the hotel front desk can point you to the nearest one.
2. Grab cedis, but do not change everything at once

Most ATMs at Kotoka dispense Ghana cedis on Visa and Mastercard. Take enough for the first two days: taxi, tips, a meal, some SIM credit. Change the rest at a forex bureau in town the next day. Bureau rates in Osu, Cantonments or East Legon are usually better than the airport counter, and small denominations are gold for street food and trotro fares.
Cards work in supermarkets, fuel stations and most restaurants. Cash still rules at chop bars, markets, and most taxis.
3. Use the ride apps. They work.

Bolt, Uber and Yango all operate in Accra. The first ride from the airport is the one to take with the official airport taxi desk if it is late and you are tired. After that, the apps are cheaper and the route is tracked on your phone. Save your hotel as a favourite destination on day one so future rides are one tap.
A koach tip. At rush hour, some drivers will call to renegotiate the fare the app quoted. Decline politely and order another. The second one almost always honours the price.
4. Eat something Ghanaian before you sleep

Jet lag listens to food. Skip the room service and ask the front desk for the nearest spot serving jollof, waakye or grilled tilapia with banku. A plate of waakye with shito and a cold sobolo is one of the kindest things you can do to a tired body. If your hotel is in Osu, Buka and Asanka Local are both reliable for that first night. In Airport Residential, +233 Jazz Bar & Grill keeps food going late.
This is the small moment a lot of returners write home about.
5. Walk one block before bed

Even ten minutes will do. The night air, the generators humming, the security guard who tells you "you are welcome" because that is how people greet you here. That walk is when Accra stops being an idea and starts being a place you are in.
What the koach handles for you

If TripKoach is planning your trip, your first 24 hours are already covered. Airport pickup waiting with your name, the SIM sorted, a cedis float in the welcome pack, and a koach on WhatsApp from the moment your wheels touch down. title: Akwaaba to the green season: why May to July is one of the best times to come to Ghana
excerpt: Yes, it rains. It is also when Boti Falls runs full, Aburi turns a deeper green, prices drop, and the crowds thin out. Here is what the green season actually looks like, and how TripKoach keeps you covered.
heroAlt: Boti Falls in full flow, surrounded by lush green canopy in the Eastern Region of Ghana.
author: TripKoach

body.x: Most travel guides will tell you to come to Ghana in December. They are not wrong, Detty December is loud, joyful, and unforgettable. But if you ask a koach, the months almost no one talks about, May, June, and July, are some of the most beautiful, peaceful, and affordable times to visit.
We call it the green season. And it is genuinely worth your trip.
Yes, it rains. Here is what that actually means.

The rains in southern Ghana usually fall in heavy bursts, often an hour or two in the late afternoon, and then the sun is back. Mornings stay bright. Evenings cool down to a perfect 24 to 26 °C. You will not be hiking through a downpour all day, and you will not be sweating through every shirt.
What rain does give you:

x: Waterfalls in full flow. Boti Falls, Wli, Kintampo and Tsenku all hit their peak in May and June. The dry-season trickle becomes a wall of water.
Lush, photo-ready landscapes. Aburi Botanical Gardens, the Eastern Region hills, and the Volta cliffs turn a deeper, richer green than the brown haze of harmattan.
Cooler temperatures inland. No more punishing midday heat at Cape Coast or Kakum.

body.x: Where the green season shines
A few experiences land especially well in May to July:

x: Aburi & the Eastern Region, botanical gardens, bead markets at Krobo-Odumase, and the Akosombo Dam at the start of the rains.
The Volta Region, Wli Falls running full, Mount Afadja in cloud, and Tafi Atome monkey sanctuary at its most active.
Indoor heritage stops, Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park, the W.E.B. Du Bois Centre, Manhyia Palace in Kumasi. Rain-proof, story-rich, and refreshingly uncrowded.
Kakum & Cape Coast, green canopy walk, cooler castles, and the historical weight of the slave forts without the December queue.

body.x: What to pack (short list)

x: A light rain jacket or compact umbrella, not a heavy one
Quick-dry travel pants and two pairs of grippy walking shoes
A dry-bag for your phone and passport
Insect repellent with DEET (mosquitoes are more active when it is wet)
One smart-casual outfit for evenings in Accra

body.x: That is it. We handle the rest on the ground.
Why this is the moment

On 8 May, the Ghana Tourism Authority launched their new "Experience Ghana" campaign, a national push to invite visitors and the diaspora to share the country authentically. The timing is not an accident. Hotels, restaurants, and tour operators are leaning into low-season hospitality: better rates, more attentive service, and easier access to the experiences that get fully booked in December.

You also get something December cannot give you: space. Empty viewing platforms at Boti. A quiet morning at the Cape Coast Castle. A market in Makola where the sellers have time to teach you a Twi word.
#WeHaveGotYouCovered

Rainy-season travel in Ghana works when the logistics are handled. That is the whole point of a koach. We watch the radar, swap an outdoor itinerary for an indoor one when a storm rolls in, and put you in a 4×4 with Wi-Fi when the road to a waterfall gets muddy. Medical doctor on call, 24/7 on-ground support, and a team that has done this in every month of the year.
It is a return. It is also, quietly, a really good trip.

title: Is Ghana safe? An honest answer for first-time visitors
excerpt: The short answer: yes, and here's the honest, on-the-ground context behind it.
heroAlt: View of the Tema harbour skyline with cranes silhouetted against the Ghanaian coast.
author: TripKoach

body.x: The short answer
Yes, Ghana is one of the safest countries to visit in West Africa.

It is politically stable, English-speaking, and has welcomed travelers, students, and returning Diaspora for decades. The Global Peace Index consistently ranks Ghana among the most peaceful nations on the continent, and the country's "Year of Return" and "Beyond the Return" programs have brought hundreds of thousands of international visitors home, most of whom describe Ghana with one word: Akwaaba. Welcome.
But "safe" is not the same as "no awareness needed." So let's give you the honest picture.
What makes Ghana feel safe

x: Stable democracy. Peaceful elections, no active conflict, and a constitution older than many in the region.
English everywhere. Signage, customer service, hospitals, ride-hailing, you can navigate without a translator.
Hospitality is a value, not a slogan. Ghanaians are famously welcoming. Strangers will help you find your way, and elders will greet you in the street.
Tourism infrastructure that actually works. Hotels, licensed guides, registered transport, mobile money, and reliable airports in Accra and Kumasi.
Healthcare access. Private hospitals in Accra and major cities meet international standards. (Trip Koach guests get a medical doctor on call.)

body.x: What to be aware of (the same as any new country)

x: Petty theft in crowded markets. Keep your phone in your front pocket at Makola or Kejetia, just like you would in Rome or New York.
Traffic in Accra. Roads are busy and pedestrian crossings are informal, cross with locals, not alone.
Scams targeting tourists. Unsolicited "guides" at the airport or beach promising free tours are best politely declined. Book through a licensed operator.
Health prep matters. Yellow fever vaccination is required for entry. Malaria prophylaxis is recommended. Drink bottled or filtered water.
Photography etiquette. Always ask before photographing people, and never photograph government buildings, military, or border posts.

body.x: How Trip Koach keeps it stress-free
We don't just tell you Ghana is safe, we structure your trip so safety is built in from the moment you land:

x: Airport pickup by a verified driver who knows your flight
24/7 on-ground support, in your language
Pre-booked accommodations vetted for security and comfort
Local SIM/eSIM so you're connected from minute one
Medical doctor on call (consultation covered)
A koach who texts you when you arrive, when you check in, and any time you have a question

body.x: #WeHaveGotYouCovered
Bottom line

title: Safety precautions to consider when visiting Ghana
excerpt: Ghana is safe and welcoming, but a little preparation turns a good trip into a great one. Here's the practical checklist.
heroAlt: A TripKoach guide in a colonial-era helmet saluting inside a historical Ghanaian armoury.
author: TripKoach

body.x: Ghana is one of the most welcoming countries you'll ever visit, but smart travel is always prepared travel. Whether it's your first trip or your fifth, this is the practical, lived-in checklist we share with every Trip Koach guest before they fly.
Before you fly

x: Confirm your yellow fever vaccination. It's required for entry. Carry the yellow card with your passport.
Start malaria prophylaxis as prescribed by your doctor (typically 1 to 2 days before arrival).
Get travel insurance that covers medical evacuation. Don't skip this.
Photocopy your passport, visa, and yellow card. Keep one copy in your luggage and email a copy to yourself.
Register with your embassy if your home country offers a traveler registration program.
Tell your bank you're traveling. Otherwise the first ATM withdrawal in Accra will be declined.

body.x: On arrival at Kotoka (Accra)

x: Pre-arrange your pickup. Don't accept rides from people approaching you in the terminal, use a verified driver (Trip Koach or a registered taxi service).
Buy a local SIM or activate an eSIM before you leave the airport so you're connected immediately.
Withdraw cash at the bank ATM inside the terminal, not from kiosks outside.
Keep your passport on your person for the first 24 hours; you'll need it for hotel check-in and SIM registration.

body.x: Daily habits that keep you safe

x: Carry small notes. Cedi 5s, 10s, and 20s, vendors and taxi drivers rarely have change for large bills.
Use mobile money (MoMo). It's everywhere and cuts down on cash handling.
Drink only sealed bottled or filtered water. Avoid ice unless you know it's filtered.
Eat where it's busy. Crowded chop bars and restaurants turn over food quickly, that's a good sign.
Cover up at dusk. Long sleeves and trousers reduce mosquito bites; combine with DEET-based repellent.
Dress with a little modesty in rural and northern areas. Shoulders and knees covered shows respect.

body.x: Money, scams, and street smarts

x: Agree on the fare before getting in a taxi, or use Bolt/Uber where they operate (Accra, Kumasi, Takoradi).
Politely decline unsolicited "guides" at attractions, beaches, or the airport. A friendly "no thank you" works.
Never pay a "fee" to anyone in uniform without an official receipt. Real fees are documented.
Keep your phone in your front pocket in crowded markets like Makola (Accra) or Kejetia (Kumasi).
Leave valuables in the hotel safe and carry only what you need for the day.

body.x: Photography & cultural respect

x: Always ask before photographing people. A simple "Please, may I?" is enough.
Never photograph the airport, military, police, or government buildings. This is taken seriously.
At cultural sites and shrines, follow your guide's lead on what is and isn't allowed.
Greet first, transact second. A "Good morning, how are you?" before asking for directions or pricing changes the whole interaction.

body.x: Health & emergencies

x: Save these numbers the day you arrive:
Police: 191
Ambulance: 193
Fire: 192
Your hotel front desk
Your koach (Trip Koach guests get a 24/7 number)
Know your nearest hospital. In Accra, ask your koach to brief you on the closest private facility.
Carry a small first-aid kit with rehydration salts, antidiarrheals, and any prescriptions in original packaging.

body.x: Driving and getting around

x: Don't self-drive on your first trip. Ghana's roads are safe but the rhythm takes practice. Use a hired driver, ride-hail, or your tour transport.
Avoid intercity travel after dark. Roads outside the cities are not always lit.
Wear a seatbelt every time, even in taxis. It's the law and the right call.

title: Why visit Ghana? 9 reasons this country stays with you
excerpt: From the Cape Coast castles to Kakum's canopy walk, here's why Ghana keeps showing up on every traveler's bucket list, and why those who come, come back.
heroAlt: The 'Last Bath' memorial archway at Assin Manso, the final freshwater stop for enslaved Africans before being marched to the Cape Coast slave forts.
author: TripKoach

body.x: Ask anyone who's been to Ghana what struck them most, and you'll hear the same things over and over: the warmth of the people, the depth of the history, the rhythm of daily life. Ghana doesn't try to impress you, it simply welcomes you in, and you leave changed.
Here are nine reasons it should be on your list.
1. The history runs deeper than any guidebook

Cape Coast Castle. Elmina Castle. The Door of No Return. Standing in these places, where millions of Africans were forced through into the transatlantic slave trade, is one of the most important journeys a person can make. Ghana doesn't sanitize this history. It honors it, and invites you to honor it too.
For the African Diaspora, this is more than tourism. It is a return.
2. Akwaaba is not a slogan

"Akwaaba", welcome in Twi, is the first word you'll hear and the one you'll remember. Ghanaians are warm, curious, generous with their time, and proud of their country. Strangers will help you find an address. Elders will greet you in the street. Children will wave from doorways.
Hospitality here is a value, not a service standard.
3. Heritage and homecoming

The Year of Return (2019) brought hundreds of thousands of Diasporans home for the first time. Beyond the Return continues that work. Whether you're tracing ancestry, attending the Panafest, or simply walking the streets of Jamestown, Ghana offers something rare: a place where you don't have to explain who you are.
4. Landscapes that go far beyond the beach

x: Kakum National Park, the canopy walkway, 30 meters above the rainforest floor.
Mole National Park, elephants, antelope, and savannah safaris in the north.
Lake Volta, one of the largest man-made lakes in the world.
Wli Falls, the tallest waterfall in West Africa, hidden in the Volta hills.
Busua and Ada beaches, Atlantic surf, palm trees, and grilled tilapia at sunset.

body.x: Ghana is small enough to see a lot in two weeks, and large enough that you'll plan a second trip before you leave.
5. The food will surprise you

Jollof rice (and yes, the Jollof Wars are real, Ghana's wins). Waakye for breakfast. Fresh tilapia and banku by the coast. Kelewele, fried plantains with ginger and chili, that you'll be thinking about for months. Suya from a roadside grill. Palm nut soup that tastes like home, even if you've never been home before.
Eat where it's busy. Trust your nose.
6. Music, fashion, and a creative scene that's exporting

Afrobeats, highlife, hiplife, Ghana's sound is everywhere right now. Designers in Osu and Labadi are shaping global fashion. Accra's gallery and film scenes are some of the most exciting on the continent. You can spend an evening at a rooftop bar in Cantonments and meet writers, founders, and DJs who are building what comes next.
7. Festivals worth flying for

x: Homowo (Ga people, August/September), a celebration of the harvest with kpekple and a procession through Accra.
Aboakyer (Winneba, May), the deer hunt festival.
Panafest (Cape Coast, biennial), pan-African theater, music, and reconciliation.
Afrochella / Afro Future (December), the music festival that put modern Accra on the global map.
Chale Wote (James Town, August), street art, performance, and design takes over the historic neighborhood.

body.x: If you can plan around one, do.
8. It's accessible, in every sense

x: English is the official language. You'll navigate without a translator.
Visa-on-arrival is available for many nationalities, and the e-Visa makes the rest easy.
Direct flights from New York, London, Amsterdam, Brussels, Istanbul, Addis, and most of West Africa.
The cedi stretches further than you'd expect, Ghana is excellent value for the experience you get.
Mobile money, eSIM, and ride-hailing all work the way you expect.

That's why we exist. Trip Koach is a Ghana-based travel company that combines local knowledge with international service standards. We handle airport pickup, accommodations, transport, connectivity, and a 24/7 koach who answers when you call.
You bring the curiosity. We bring the rest.

title: Basic language words to learn before / on arrival
excerpt: Greet people or say a few words and locals will admire and welcome you warmly, useful when you're shopping, touring, or strolling Osu Oxford Street.
heroAlt: A TripKoach guide explaining a wood-carving tree to travelers at Aburi Botanical Gardens, Eastern Region.
author: TripKoach

body.x: The Twi language is widely spoken in almost all regions of Ghana. In the Greater Accra Region, the main local language is Ga, the mother tongue of the people of Accra.

Since Accra is the capital city, and your arrival airport, learning a few basic local words goes a long way. Ghanaians truly appreciate it when visitors make an effort to speak their language, even just a little.

When you can greet people or say simple words, sellers and locals will admire and welcome you warmly. This is especially useful when you're shopping, touring, or interacting with people around Osu Oxford Street, the Arts Centre of Ghana, or Makola Market.
Speaking a few local words will make your experience more enjoyable, friendly, and memorable.
